Interviewer:	I'll tell you a bit about what we're doing to begin with. We're interviewing women from all the different engineering departments. Are you going on the industrial placement? (yeah) We're mainly interviewing people that are going on placement, but we are also interviewing a few that aren't going on placement. We're interviewing people to find out why they've decided to do engineering, what they expect to get from the placement and then we're going to go back to people on the placement as well. But, at the end of it all we're going to put a report together and give it to the Engineering Council and hopefully it will help to improve the situation, for women, in the industry. So I'll start off asking you a few questions about your background and why you decided to go into engineering, things like that. Is it a commercial management and quantity surveying that you're doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you do A levels?

Subject:	Yes, I did.

Interviewer:	What A levels?

Subject:	Yeah, but I did a Ugandan certificate, more like GCSE or A levels – it's one of those er well I just like (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, did you do any particular subjects?

Subject:	Yeah, I did mathematics, economics and geography at (?) Yeah, so they considered my mathematics and economics.

Interviewer:	When did you come to the UK? When you started at the university or were you here before that?

Subject:	Well I come, I looked at university, the year before but then I was like asked to come, to study, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to? Was it a mixed school or an all girls school?

Subject:	Mixed school. There was a ratio of 1:5 – 1 girl, 5 boys, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, so you're quite used to being in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, what do your parents do? Are either of them engineers?

Subject:	No, not really, my dad is just a manufacturer. Well neither of my parents is an engineer.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide to study engineering?

Subject:	Erm, at my A levels, when we were choosing what course to do, I decided to do something to do with construction, basically because my dad had a construction firm at one point. So I was like oh let me just try doing construction.

Interviewer:	Yeah. What do you think it was about construction that you found interesting?

Subject:	Er, I had options, I wanted to do Quantity Surveying and then I wanted to – it's like – and the people who do such courses back home are usually – well are very rich, so I was like maybe that would be my kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing any other types of engineering like mechanical or manufacturing engineering?

Subject:	Maybe electrical at one time but I was – this came, this is (?) construction.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decided to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Well my sister had been – had been in England before and she was – we looked up the (?) so what criteria it has for engineering – and found out it was one of the best (?) that was good at – and because it had a sandwich course – that really was, it appealed to me, so I thought I'd apply for that.

Interviewer:	OK, How did you decide to come to the UK to study? Did you always want to do that?

Subject:	Yeah, I always wanted to do that and er, improve on my qualifications and things like that and because most of my family has been here. So yeah, and it's quite secure and everything, so I was like why not come here?

Interviewer:	OK, did it ever bother you that engineering was so male dominated?

Subject:	Not really 'cos I've come up in a family that my father keeps telling us we're the same as male and all that kind of stuff. And I grow up and I want to be an engineer – I have to prove that I'm better than male because, for my first – for my A levels, I was – we were 4 girls and 90 boys like in my course, which I was doing for my A levels. So that didn't put me down really and I wanted to do this, really.

Interviewer:	Was that just the subjects that you had chosen that were so…?

Subject:	It was the subjects. Most girls didn't take those subjects and it was also the environment of the school. Yeah, basically, there were fewer girls than boys.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah. More – at least (that would reduce the tension?) because usually when we're asked about, or if you're on site and you're a woman, what will you do, if this happens and that kind of thing? So if more women came into the engineering sector, (lost words) can do this or they can do that.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that there aren't more women?

Subject:	First of all, for my course, quantity surveying and commercial management. Basically women aren't like attracted to doing some kind of jobs, like – or going on site and all that kind of thing, they'd prefer being in an office and those kinds of things. But if they see there was more to that than being on site, because someone can be in a consultancy and still be in the office really and just go on site (lost words), sometimes. So maybe that would attract more woman to the site and then er maybe she'd look – they shouldn't make the course look really complicated, like building or that kind of thing. Then maybe more women would come onto it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women don't do engineering because they don't really know what it is? They think it is all on site?

Subject:	Yeah, They don't really know about engineering.

Interviewer:	What do you think would help to encourage more women?

Subject:	Well, the thing is that like for example when I tried to get into my course, it was the commercial bit. I was like – is that commercial management – that attracted me. It looked like – oh, I can do this. I think that if I don't do well in the engineering sector, I do the commercial bit. I mean the modules they will show all these computing – there is erm all technology and all that kind of thing. So I was interested in all that because it shows it's just more than like going onto site, more than building – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer or construction worker?

Subject:	Worker or are you specifying woman?

Interviewer:	No, any. 

Subject:	Any. Er, being flexible really. Being honest and friendly – you have to get to know people, doing team work, being (?) so much and then being motivated.

Interviewer:	OK Do you think that any of those characteristics you would say are more male or more female?

Subject:	Erm, not really I don't think so.

Interviewer:	That's OK. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Yeah, as I said back it is – really all my (??) or your own man in a way, being on site. It can mean making a noise and all that kind of thing but if it is a boy, no one is ever bothered about it really. That's the only disadvantage from that really. I mean there was another course – another interview which I went for a placement, and I was taken on because I was a woman – that's what they say, because the job is in Botswana and they say – basically in Africa construction and engineering is dominated by male and he couldn't put me on site because I was a woman – fearing for my situation on site and anything could happen to me. So it's one of the divisions here.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages?

Subject:	Mm, advantages? Well, at the moment, they're promoting women to go onto site and do engineering, it's an advantage to be able to get jobs quite faster, sometimes.

Interviewer:	OK, we'll talk a bit about the course now. Has it been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Mm, er well it's been quite interesting, I guess, because I've learnt lots of new things and I've made new friends and everything like that from the course, which is really good.

Interviewer:	How many girls are there on the course?

Subject:	3.

Interviewer:	3 out of how many?

Subject:	Like 40 boys. We are 3 girls – we are 3 girls out of 40 boys, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. And what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Well the boys really. You can't keep the work (lost words) like in the beginning that's what they used to do – like give the girls more work to do. And then, we kind of get to learn from them, as it gets like from you, which is a good thing really.

Interviewer:	Yeah any bad things?

Subject:	Well it's like being (?) here all the work – I mean they take you for granted that you're going to keep doing the work, because you're a girl and that kind of thing. So it is quite a lot really and then bad things on the course – it's sort of like a physical thing but it's things which are quite strenuous to do like surveying a whole day (sitting?) and climbing up rocks and all that kind of thing. So that it's strenuous but you can overcome it by being fit.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	No – 1, 2.

Interviewer:	2?

Subject:	They took (?) lectures

Interviewer:	Do you think that they had a different style to the male lecturers? Did they teach different types of subjects?

Subject:	Mm, they did teach different types of subjects, but then er – yeah, the female teachers taught different types of subjects but the same thing really but just teaching all different. We had 2 in the last – it was my first year. Yeah

Interviewer:	What did the female lecturers take you for?

Subject:	Pardon?

Interviewer:	What subjects did they take you for?

Subject:	Erm, measurements – they did measurements for us (but I didn't understand it?) I wasn't – well, the ones that I prefer actually, for this last 2 years, 2 years have been likely to be male lecturers, yeah, because the female lecturers tend to make it look like all you have to do is just learn this thing and that kind of thing and then they don't want it to – it's all different really, that's all I can say.

Interviewer:	OK, would you have liked to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	And why do you think that is? Is it like encouraging in that…?

Subject:	Yeah, it is kind of they are role models. They tend to be – because there's some female lecturers, who really just don't care but then there's some who are really – who acted like role models and encouraged you to do something. But some are (listed?) – really aren't that bothered whether they're female or male.

Interviewer:	OK, have the male lecturers treated you the same as the male students, do you think?

Subject:	Yeah, they have, they have. Just the same.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male?

Subject:	Female.

Interviewer:	Are they approachable or would you rather have a different personal tutor?

Subject:	Will I be held against this? (Laugh) Well …

Interviewer:	It's all confidential.

Subject:	OK, well there's someone – I've had a – my, my female tutor's not really been that good – really she isn't kind – because one time I told her, in my first year there were boys who were harassing me, like basically they'd end up giving me work and that kind of thing and they were really not good. Well I told her about it and she was just like, well it will pass like – something of that sort. She didn't even call them to talk to them or that kind of thing. It wasn't encouraging really. And sometimes when you're having a hard time with your course and modules and all that kind of thing, usually, my friends usually go up to their personal tutors and they encourage them but this one doesn't do that. So I would – it's not – it's not because she's female or what but, but I think I prefer the male tutors because they treat you like, or they tell me take this course, you're determined to do – so they help you up. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is there any possibility that you can change – that your personal tutor changes at all?

Subject:	I don't know. I'm not sure about if I can have my personal tutor changed really. Yeah. I usually refer to my one who heads my course – yeah, he's very encouraging and all that kind of thing, yeah.

Interviewer:	You said about other people giving you all the work to do, was that when you were doing group work?

Subject:	Yeah, group work.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do a lot of group work?

Subject:	Yeah, a lot of group work.

Interviewer:	OK, when you're working in groups, do you get put into groups or do you choose who you want to work with?

Subject:	Er, sometimes you're put into groups and sometimes you choose who to work with.

Interviewer:	When you get to choose yourself, how do you decide who to work with?

Subject:	Well, people who you know or really who you want to work with. That's how you choose the people you want to work with.

Interviewer:	Do you work with other girls or…?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	That's alright, do you want to tell me about the bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Pardon?

Interviewer:	The bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Yeah, well the bad experiences of group work is usually the first time when I was in my first year really, when all the work would be given to you and end up – and only when you're going away for the weekend and all that kind of thing, and you can't hand in the coursework. Or you keep calling the group – you're group mates – and they don't turn up a week, to hand in your course work, or some send emails and they claim they don't receive their emails. I mean you arrange meetings and no-one comes, those were the bad times of group work really. And then sometimes they don't really want to do any work. And then after the work's been done they claim that you didn't try to get hold of them.

Interviewer:	Do you think that situation is worse because you're working with males? Do you think females would be different or just the same?

Subject:	 (long pause) Well, I think it's 80% because they don't (lost words) they're male and then some females don't even know what they're doing, because of what happens in the area – they don't tend to do their work and kind of, so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are benefits or advantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, you get to learn things and work is going very fast. And then your motivated to do work of (lost words)

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think that the group work will help you when you go to work, as well?

Subject:	Yeah, they say its got to help because you've tried out work but you see – you get to work with people and all that kind of thing and you do that in the construction industry. Yeah, it's all about team work.

Interviewer:	OK, are there any bits of teaching or advice that you've had that you think will help you when you're on your placement?

Subject:	Yeah, a lot. Well working in teams and all the – some of the modules that I've worked upon, they'll be helpful and then getting to meet new people because well this course, I've learnt knowing people and about people, and being patient with people, so that could be something that will help me when I'm on site – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement?

Subject:	Well, er, I think I've been given a good picture about what's going to be in store and we have tutorials and that kind of thing. But like when you're in site and you're a woman, and all that kind of thing, can be quite scary and at the moment I don't know exactly where I'm going to be placed 'cos of the company's given 3 weeks notice til they tell me. It's a bit annoying really but their meant to be giving us a presentation in 2 weeks time so that would be very helpful

Interviewer:	Do you know who you're going to work for?

Subject:	Yeah I do.

Interviewer:	What company?

Subject:	 [Name].

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the university could do more to help prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Prepare me for placement?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Yeah, they could do more help you prepare for placement. I mean they don't encourage like – for example my course is a sponsored course and all that kind of thing. I mean like for other places like chemical engineering (yeah) the department helps them get the placements, so it's quite helpful. Whereas we have to go out and get a placement ourselves which is quite difficult really. Like other departments like chemical engineering which is a bit encouraging, they help the students get the placement – they help employers get in contact with the students, which is very good. But well with my course and most of my department, usually we have to go out of way to do all that – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, you said about your course being sponsored, are you a sponsored student?

Subject:	No I'm not.

Interviewer:	No. Did you ever consider getting a sponsorship?

Subject:	Yeah, but it's quite difficult at the moment really, because its hard to get any placements – so it would be hard to get sponsorship. But then I'm trying to like – if I go on this placement maybe I'll do – maybe I'll get sponsorship for the final year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages to getting a sponsorship?

Subject:	Yeah, disadvantages to sponsorship? Mm, well you get lazy because just no – yeah, I'm being catered for. Most students are like that on my course because they are sponsored, they are like we don't really care but well, I at the moment 'cos my parent's are paying for the tuition fees and the sponsorship and everything – it's a bit difficult, they have to really work extremely hard, yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok, why did you decide that you wanted to go on a placement?

Subject:	Because of the work – I needed work experience, I had no clue what I was doing. And then I just kept learning these things – but I wanted to put them into practice. So I decided to go on placement.

Interviewer:	OK, did you apply to lots of companies?

Subject:	Yes, I did.

Interviewer:	Did you have any particular criteria when you were choosing which company to apply to?

Subject:	Well, I was given a list of the companies to apply to and I kept applying to them, you know, generally (lost words) and applying to them, but then with time you have to be patient. I was replied - when was it - much of them were full and I was applying in November, so yes, it took a long time.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the company?

Subject:	Yeah, I did, I just used the web site, I just used the careers office and I asked my heads of department about the companies.

Interviewer:	OK, when you were looking at the companies did you concentrate on things like how much you were going to get paid and whether there were any career prospects once you'd finished the course?

Subject:	Yeah, I was looking at the career prospects and I was looking at the – like the line of (?) they give to being chartered – chartership and all that. And then I was – I wasn't looking at the salary really, because at the moment I'm just thinking I need – what can I do to get work experience? That's what I'm thinking at the moment. So – 'cos I really want to (?) whereas if I'd just come back and said take me, (lost words) because I really wanted to learn more to do with construction, 'cos I'd just spend on many more modules without doing any experience about it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you'll be able to use what you learn, when you're on placement, when you come back for your final year?

Subject:	Yeah I guess I'll be able to choose my dissertation more appropriately. So I guess, so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Well, first of all, I'll be having no idea of where I'm going to be going, so looking for my accommodation and all that, I'm dreading all that but then it's like a new learning experience, you see, and it's – it'll help me to understand where I'm going – and all that kind of thing. Mmm, if I'm on site and it's cold and things like that. I'm not looking forward to that. And the rest – I'm excited about the rest really. I want to learn more of the things, yeah.

Interviewer:	Earlier you mentioned about being a woman on the site, are you worried about that at all?

Subject:	Not really, because I used to work – before coming here I used to work among my dad's company and it was male dominated, I was among all males, so I'm not really bothered about it now.

Interviewer:	Ok, that's fine. Do you know anything about what you will be doing when you're on placement? Do you know yet whether you'll be on site or not?

Subject:	No, I don't know

Interviewer:	How do you think that being at work will be different from being at university?

Subject:	Well I'll be waking up at 7 O'clock, I guess, will be at work, whereas at University you just wake up when you have lectures – and er it's going to be different because my life will be (?) and all that kind of thing and then erm (lost words) I will be doing things at a particular time and all week you'll have to be working and (?) and all that so it's going to be really different.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that you'll get treated differently?

Subject:	Well I guess so because they won't expect me to have learnt everything – I have no clue about some things because I have the knowledge but then I have to put it into practice, so I guess they'll be able to help me out and when I get wrong – yeah, 'cos I will show you.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, what do you think that you'll be doing in 5 years time?

Subject:	Well I guess I'm going to specialise in consultancies and maybe commercial management and property and all that – yeah, that's what I want to specialise in.

Interviewer:	OK. And what about say in 10 years time? Do you think you'll be doing the same thing?

Subject:	10 years time? Well I'd like to be self-employed in 10 years time.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what appeals to you about that?

Subject:	Oh, well you get to do your own work and it's more – er more motivating and more, you get to learn things on your own and you get control of things. So I'd like to do that for a while. Yeah.

Interviewer:	What would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Well, working in a consultancy – self employed. (yeah) Yeah, having my own consultancy – being self employed.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you can achieve that or do you think there'll be any difficulties trying to achieve that?

Subject:	It's going to be very difficult but then I'll have to achieve it really. It's why – it's like follow your career, goals and you have to achieve.

Interviewer:	Ok, Do you think you'll work in the UK when you've finished or…?

Subject:	Well, if I work with er [company] and they'd like to take me on, yeah I'd like to work for them for another 5 years.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what about in the future? Would you like to travel or go back home?

Subject:	Well, I'd like to travel after I've finished for maybe – I'd like to travel more (lost words) and I'd like to travel when I work – that's what I would like to do. I would like to be put on projects in different areas and (places all over the world?) that's why I actually took up this course, because you get – if you're working for a multi-national company you just (shove off?)

Interviewer:	Are [company] multi national?

Subject:	Yeah, so I'd like to do that with them.

Interviewer:	It sounds really good. Do you think that the career prospects are good in construction?

Subject:	Hmm , well sometimes the construction industry is not predictable really because sometimes you could have a boom and then sometimes you go bust. So you never know really what will happen. Yeah – but then, because – in (?) because of properties coming up (lost words) so I guess it's quite a good career – mm.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? If you wanted to do it all again, would you do anything differently?

Subject:	No I wouldn't do anything different. It would be in the same area because – yeah – because if I've – I mean if I'm architect, but then it's the same thing really, just because I'm doing the commercial route really, so I wouldn't change my career.

Interviewer:	OK, that's good. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the construction industry? 

Subject:	Sometimes exciting. Mmmmmmmmm, Boring in a way because – because you're doing the right thing all the while and er it's quite interesting, you get to learn new things and then I've had to – mmm, (laughs) let's see – er, I think sometimes you get to travel and do so many things. Yeah, and then there's a lot of team work.

Interviewer:	OK, would you describe it as male dominated?

Subject:	Would I describe it as male dominated?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	In a way, I would. Yeah, because most women are not interested in going onto site, there's only a few women on site so basically, even nowadays its hard to get a job because you're female, or if you're on site what will you do if people came round you and they're male and they tell you (sign up this?) and they take advantage of you, that kind of thing, you know, and give you so – I think it's the world we live in.

Interviewer:	Does it worry you that things like that might happen?

Subject:	Not really, no 'cos I come from a country that's male dominated. It really is. So I have my (?) I know what I want and no-one can stop me.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will stay a male dominated industry or do you think that the situation will get better for women?

Subject:	Mm, fewer men are taking up the course really. If more women took up more of the construction industry it would be less intimidating and all that type of thing. But the thing is that you can see that most people who come onto the course are mainly male, which isn't encouraging – 'cos if more female were encouraged to go to the course, and more female like – balanced with the male, it would be good really but then now, at the moment, there are more males so – it would be quite some time. But then females should find the gap (lost words).

Interviewer:	So do you think we need to start in lower education, like at primary and secondary school?

Subject:	Yeah, and then it's encouraging women and it's encouraging female that's construction, you know, that's its not all dirty and that they can do things.

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything thank you very much.
